claim: H3K36R mutants pupate at significantly reduced frequency compared to histone wild type (HWT) control animals.
source: As previously reported, H3K36R (K36R) mutants pupate at significantly reduced frequency compared to histone wild type (HWT) control animals, and fail to eclose into adults with 100% penetrance, despite exhibiting no obvious cell proliferation defects (McKay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McKay et al., 2015, which provides published evidence for this phenotype.

claim: H3K36R mutants fail to eclose into adults with 100% penetrance.
source: As previously reported, H3K36R (K36R) mutants pupate at significantly reduced frequency compared to histone wild type (HWT) control animals, and fail to eclose into adults with 100% penetrance, despite exhibiting no obvious cell proliferation defects (McKay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McKay et al., 2015, which provides published evidence for this phenotype.

claim: H3K36R mutants exhibit no obvious cell proliferation defects.
source: As previously reported, H3K36R (K36R) mutants pupate at significantly reduced frequency compared to histone wild type (HWT) control animals, and fail to eclose into adults with 100% penetrance, despite exhibiting no obvious cell proliferation defects (McKay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McKay et al., 2015, which provides published evidence for this observation.

claim: Genes with high H3K36me3 density tend to decrease expression in K36R animals.
source: Genes with high H3K36me3 density tended to decrease expression in K36R animals, whereas genes with low H3K36me3 density tended to increase expression in K36R animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the poly-A RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2A and 2B, which show the relationship between H3K36me3 density and gene expression changes.

claim: Genes with low H3K36me3 density tend to increase expression in K36R animals.
source: Genes with high H3K36me3 density tended to decrease expression in K36R animals, whereas genes with low H3K36me3 density tended to increase expression in K36R animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the poly-A RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2A and 2B, which show the relationship between H3K36me3 density and gene expression changes.

claim: H3K36me3 is anticorrelated with gene expression change across the entire spectrum of H3K36me3 density.
source: Instead, when we stratified genes by H3K36me3 density (www.modencode.org), the mark was anticorrelated with gene expression change across the entire spectrum of H3K36me3 density, and largely uncorrelated with other methyl-states of H3K36 (Figure 2A, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of poly-A RNA-seq data stratified by H3K36me3 density, as shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: H3K36me3 is largely uncorrelated with other methyl-states of H3K36.
source: Instead, when we stratified genes by H3K36me3 density (www.modencode.org), the mark was anticorrelated with gene expression change across the entire spectrum of H3K36me3 density, and largely uncorrelated with other methyl-states of H3K36 (Figure 2A, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2A, which compares H3K36me3, H3K36me2, and H3K36me1 distributions across differentially expressed genes.

claim: H3K36me plays a global role in regulating gene expression that is not confined to H3K36me3-rich loci.
source: This finding suggests a global role for H3K36me in regulating gene expression, but one that is not confined to H3K36me3-rich loci, and therefore argues against an exclusively direct, local effect.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that gene expression changes occur across the genome, not just at H3K36me3-rich loci, as shown in the differential expression analysis.

claim: Genes that are normally silent or lowly-expressed in HWT larvae experience the largest relative increases in expression in K36R mutants.
source: That is, genes that were normally silent or lowly-expressed in HWT larvae experienced the largest relative increases in expression in K36R mutants, and highly expressed genes were preferentially reduced in K36R (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the MA plot in Figure 2C showing the relationship between HWT expression level and log2 fold change in K36R mutants.

claim: Highly expressed genes are preferentially reduced in K36R mutants.
source: That is, genes that were normally silent or lowly-expressed in HWT larvae experienced the largest relative increases in expression in K36R mutants, and highly expressed genes were preferentially reduced in K36R (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the MA plot in Figure 2C showing the relationship between HWT expression level and log2 fold change in K36R mutants.

claim: H4 acetylation levels are robustly increased in H3K36R mutants.
source: In contrast, H4ac levels were robustly increased (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), confirming the previously identified link between H3K36me and H4ac (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K27me3 levels are slightly reduced in H3K36 mutants.
source: H3K27me3 levels were slightly reduced in H3K36 mutants (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), however characteristic polycomb target genes were largely unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Characteristic polycomb target genes are largely unaffected in H3K36R mutants.
source: H3K27me3 levels were slightly reduced in H3K36 mutants (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), however characteristic polycomb target genes were largely unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of polycomb target gene expression shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: H4K12ac intensity is anticorrelated with DAPI bright bands in both HWT and K36R mutants.
source: In both HWT and K36R mutants, we found that H4K12ac intensity was anticorrelated with DAPI bright bands (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining of polytene chromosomes shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hyperacetylation in K36R mutants occurs in the more actively transcribed (DAPI dark) regions.
source: Therefore, the observed hyperacetylation in K36R mutants occurs in the more actively transcribed (DAPI dark) regions, consistent with previous observations (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that H4K12ac is anticorrelated with DAPI bright bands, combined with the knowledge that DAPI bright regions correspond to transcriptionally silent chromatin, and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Global changes in open chromatin are minimal between HWT and H3K36R animals.
source: When we quantified HWT and K36R ATAC-seq signal from such a window surrounding all obsTSSs, we found that global changes in open chromatin were minimal between HWT and H3K36R animals (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3B, which shows high correlation between HWT and K36R ATAC-seq signal at transcription start sites.

claim: Chromatin remodeling at promoters is not a major contributor to the observed global gene expression changes in H3K36R mutants.
source: These results indicate that chromatin remodeling at promoters is not a major contributor to the observed global gene expression changes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ATAC-seq changes at promoters do not correlate with gene expression changes.

claim: Thousands of novel unannotated TSSs (nuTSSs) are spread throughout the HWT genome, including a large proportion located within H3K36me3-enriched exons.
source: By quantifying Start-seq signal at loci outside of annotated start-sites (obsTSSs), we identified thousands of novel unannotated TSSs (nuTSSs) spread throughout the HWT genome, including a large proportion located within H3K36me3-enriched exons (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Start-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Exonic nuTSSs are enriched for H3K36me3 relative to intronic ones.
source: Analysis of modEncode ChIP-seq read density in 400 bp windows around each nuTSS confirmed that exonic nuTSSs are enriched for H3K36me3 relative to intronic ones (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of H3K36me3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Exonic and antisense nuTSS usage is not dramatically increased in K36R mutants.
source: Contrary to expectation, exonic and antisense nuTSS usage was not dramatically increased in K36R mutants (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Start-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4B comparing nuTSS usage between HWT and K36R mutants.

claim: H3K36me3 density is anticorrelated with change in nuTSS usage.
source: Across all nuTSSs, we found that H3K36me3 density was anticorrelated with change in nuTSS 'usage,' that is, nuTSSs with lower signal in K36R than in HWT tended to have high H3K36me3 density, and vice-versa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-E comparing H3K36me3 density with changes in nuTSS usage.

claim: Modification of replication-dependent H3K36 is not required to suppress cryptic transcription in gene bodies.
source: These results show that modification of replication-dependent H3K36 is not required to suppress cryptic transcription in gene bodies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that exonic and antisense nuTSS usage is not dramatically increased in K36R mutants, as shown by Start-seq data.

claim: Pervasive initiation in gene bodies is widespread throughout the Drosophila genome, even in the presence of H3K36me.
source: Instead, we found that pervasive initiation in gene bodies is widespread throughout the Drosophila genome, even in the presence of H3K36me.
evidence: This claim is supported by the identification of thousands of nuTSSs in the HWT genome using Start-seq data.

claim: Antisense initiation does not globally accumulate in an H3K36me3-dependent manner.
source: When we analyzed sense and antisense Start-seq reads mapping to annotated coding regions as a proxy for cryptic transcription in annotated genes, we found that antisense initiation did not globally accumulate in an H3K36me3-dependent manner (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of antisense transcription shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Increased nuTSS usage occurs almost exclusively in intergenic regions.
source: When absolute change in Start-seq signal at each nuTSS is scaled to gene length, increased nuTSS usage occurs almost exclusively in intergenic regions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4D plotting nuTSS location relative to gene boundaries versus change in Start-seq signal.

claim: Decreased nuTSS usage is most prominent in the gene body, proximal to the 3' end.
source: Decreased usage is most prominent in the gene body, proximal to the 3' end (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4D plotting nuTSS location relative to gene boundaries versus change in Start-seq signal.

claim: Very few annotated exon skipping events or retained intron events are significantly different between K36R and HWT.
source: We found that very few annotated exon skipping events or retained intron events were significantly different between K36R and HWT, and there was no discernable bias toward inclusion or exclusion (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MISO analysis of alternative splicing events shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The majority of high-confidence differential splicing events detected are mild changes (∆PSI < 0.25).
source: Additionally, the majority of high-confidence differential splicing events we detected were mild changes at best (∆PSI < 0.25), indicating that a lack of K36 modification had little effect on alternative splicing regulation in K36R mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of ∆PSI values shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lack of K36 modification has little effect on alternative splicing regulation in K36R mutants.
source: Additionally, the majority of high-confidence differential splicing events we detected were mild changes at best (∆PSI < 0.25), indicating that a lack of K36 modification had little effect on alternative splicing regulation in K36R mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that differential splicing events are rare and mild in K36R mutants.

claim: Splice junction usage is unchanged in K36R mutants.
source: For junctions meeting statistical power requirements (>20 total reads), we observed no changes in the retention ratio, meaning that splice junction usage was unchanged in K36R (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the global analysis of splice junction usage shown in Figure 5C.

claim: H3K36me plays an H3K36me-dependent role for transcriptome regulation that is independent of alternative splicing.
source: Taken together, these results support an H3K36me-dependent role for transcriptome regulation that is independent of alternative splicing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that alternative splicing is largely unaffected in K36R mutants despite widespread transcriptome changes.

claim: A group of highly-expressed genes have transcripts that are reduced in the mutant poly-A RNA fraction but not in the corresponding nuclear RNA fraction.
source: When comparing our poly-A and nuclear RNA-seq results, we identified a group of highly-expressed genes whose transcripts were reduced in the mutant poly-A RNA fraction but not in the corresponding nuclear RNA fraction (Figure 6A, see full RNA-seq results in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of poly-A and nuclear RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There are no significant changes in subcellular localization of target transcripts between HWT and K36R larvae.
source: Fractionation of nuclear and cytoplasmic RNA from HWT and K36R larvae prior to reverse transcription revealed no significant changes in subcellular localization of the targets (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that a global block to mRNA export due to H3K36R mutation is unlikely.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR analysis of nuclear and cytoplasmic RNA fractions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A global block to mRNA export due to H3K36R mutation is unlikely.
source: Fractionation of nuclear and cytoplasmic RNA from HWT and K36R larvae prior to reverse transcription revealed no significant changes in subcellular localization of the targets (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that a global block to mRNA export due to H3K36R mutation is unlikely.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that subcellular localization of target transcripts is unchanged in K36R mutants.

claim: Expression differences in poly-A RNA for highly expressed genes are restored to levels more similar to HWT in the K36R background by RNAi-mediated depletion of pacman.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, the observed expression differences in poly-A RNA for a handful of highly expressed genes were restored to levels more similar to HWT in the K36R background by RNAi-mediated depletion of pcm.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C comparing gene expression in K36R mutants with and without pacman RNAi.

claim: H3K36 contributes to post-transcriptional mRNA maturation in a manner that preserves target transcripts from exonuclease-mediated degradation.
source: These results suggest that H3K36 contributes to post-transcriptional mRNA maturation in a manner that preserves target transcripts from exonuclease-mediated degradation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that depletion of the exonuclease pacman rescues expression of downregulated genes in K36R mutants.

claim: Expression levels of K36R downregulated genes are rescued by depletion of pacman, twin, and Pop2.
source: Across a panel of K36R downregulated genes, expression levels were rescued by depletion of pcm, twin, and Pop2 (Figure 6C), but not by RNAi against Dcp2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C comparing gene expression in K36R mutants with RNAi against different RNA degradation factors.

claim: Expression levels of K36R downregulated genes are not rescued by RNAi against Dcp2.
source: Across a panel of K36R downregulated genes, expression levels were rescued by depletion of pcm, twin, and Pop2 (Figure 6C), but not by RNAi against Dcp2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B comparing gene expression in K36R mutants with and without Dcp2 RNAi.

claim: The YFP transcript displays reduced poly-A tail length in K36R mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, we found that the YFP transcript displayed reduced poly-A tail length in K36R mutants, indicative of a role for H3K36 methylation over terminal exons in recruitment or functioning of the polyadenylation machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by LM-PAT assay results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The shorter poly-A tail in K36R mutants is independent of deadenylation activity.
source: Importantly, the shorter poly-A tail in K36R mutants was independent of deadenylation activity (Figure 6D), demonstrating that the defect is in polyadenylation, not in the subsequent CCR4/twin- or CNOT7/Pop2-dependent deadenylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by LM-PAT assay results shown in Figure 6D comparing poly-A tail length in K36R mutants with and without twin RNAi.

claim: The defect in K36R mutants is in polyadenylation, not in the subsequent CCR4/twin- or CNOT7/Pop2-dependent deadenylation.
source: Importantly, the shorter poly-A tail in K36R mutants was independent of deadenylation activity (Figure 6D), demonstrating that the defect is in polyadenylation, not in the subsequent CCR4/twin- or CNOT7/Pop2-dependent deadenylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that poly-A tail length is reduced in K36R mutants even when deadenylase activity is inhibited.

claim: Poly-A site specification is largely unaffected by mutation of H3K36.
source: Computational analysis of differential poly-A site usage demonstrated no change (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), indicating that poly-A site specification was largely unaffected by mutation of H3K36.
evidence: This claim is supported by DaPars analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: H3K36 has a post-transcriptional role in the regulation of metazoan gene expression.
source: In summary, these data uncover a post-transcriptional role for H3K36 in the regulation of metazoan gene expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective observations that H3K36 affects mRNA stability through polyadenylation and sensitivity to RNA degradation pathways.

claim: Eukaryotic genomes function within the context of chromatin fibers composed of nucleosome units.
source: Eukaryotic genomes function within the context of chromatin fibers composed of nucleosome units, each of which contains roughly 147 bp of DNA wrapped around a single histone octamer composed of two pairs of heterodimers (histone H2A-H2B, and H3-H4) (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Luger et al., 1997, which provides established knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: Each nucleosome contains roughly 147 bp of DNA wrapped around a single histone octamer.
source: Eukaryotic genomes function within the context of chromatin fibers composed of nucleosome units, each of which contains roughly 147 bp of DNA wrapped around a single histone octamer composed of two pairs of heterodimers (histone H2A-H2B, and H3-H4) (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Luger et al., 1997, which provides established knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: The histone octamer is composed of two pairs of heterodimers (histone H2A-H2B, and H3-H4).
source: Eukaryotic genomes function within the context of chromatin fibers composed of nucleosome units, each of which contains roughly 147 bp of DNA wrapped around a single histone octamer composed of two pairs of heterodimers (histone H2A-H2B, and H3-H4) (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Luger et al., 1997, which provides established knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: H3K36 di- and tri-methylation (H3K36me2/3) are enriched in coding regions and toward the 3' end of actively transcribed genes.
source: In contrast with many PTMs whose spatial distribution is skewed towards promoters and the 5' regions of genes, H3K36 di- and tri-methylation (H3K36me2/3) are enriched in coding regions and toward the 3' end of actively transcribed genes (Bannister et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bannister et al., 2005, which provides published evidence for the distribution of H3K36me2/3.

claim: H3K36me2/3 marks are preferentially enriched over exons as opposed to introns.
source: These marks are also preferentially enriched over exons as opposed to introns (Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009, which provides published evidence for the exonic enrichment of H3K36me2/3.

claim: H3K36me3 suppresses cryptic transcription initiation from coding regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae by recruiting a repressive Rpd3 deacetylase complex to sites of active elongation.
source: Indeed, H3K36me2/3 is known to suppress cryptic transcription initiation from coding regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae by recruiting a repressive Rpd3 deacetylase complex to sites of active elongation (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carrozza et al., 2005 and Keogh et al., 2005, which provide published evidence for this mechanism in yeast.

claim: H3K36me3 is implicated in suppressing active incorporation of acetylated histones via histone exchange.
source: It is also implicated in suppressing active incorporation of acetylated histones via histone exchange (Venkatesh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Venkatesh et al., 2012, which provides published evidence for this mechanism.

claim: Ablation of human SETD2 is suggested to alter a number of exon inclusion events by recruiting RNA binding proteins in cultured cells.
source: In cultured cells, ablation of human SETD2, which catalyzes H3K36 trimethylation, is suggested to alter a number of exon inclusion events by recruiting RNA binding proteins (Luco et al., 2010; Pradeepa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luco et al., 2010 and Pradeepa et al., 2012, which provide published evidence for this role of SETD2.

claim: H3K36me3 distribution across gene bodies is sensitive to perturbations in splicing.
source: Conversely, H3K36me3 distribution across gene bodies is itself sensitive to perturbations in splicing (de Almeida et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Almeida et al., 2011 and Kim et al., 2011, which provide published evidence for this relationship.

claim: H3K36me has been attributed roles in X-chromosome dosage compensation.
source: In addition to its role in transcription and RNA processing, a range of other activities have been attributed to H3K36me, including X-chromosome dosage compensation (Larschan et al., 2007), DNA damage response (Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014; Pfister et al., 2014), and three dimensional chromosome organization (Evans et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; Ulianov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Larschan et al., 2007, which provides published evidence for this role.

claim: H3K36me has been attributed roles in DNA damage response.
source: In addition to its role in transcription and RNA processing, a range of other activities have been attributed to H3K36me, including X-chromosome dosage compensation (Larschan et al., 2007), DNA damage response (Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014; Pfister et al., 2014), and three dimensional chromosome organization (Evans et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; Ulianov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014; and Pfister et al., 2014, which provide published evidence for this role.

claim: H3K36me has been attributed roles in three dimensional chromosome organization.
source: In addition to its role in transcription and RNA processing, a range of other activities have been attributed to H3K36me, including X-chromosome dosage compensation (Larschan et al., 2007), DNA damage response (Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014; Pfister et al., 2014), and three dimensional chromosome organization (Evans et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; Ulianov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Evans et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; and Ulianov et al., 2016, which provide published evidence for this role.

claim: Arginine approximates the charge and steric conformation of lysine.
source: Arginine approximates the charge and steric conformation of lysine, but cannot be targeted by lysine methyltransferases, and therefore represents an appropriate mutation with which to study the PTM-specific functions of H3K36.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of amino acid properties.

claim: Arginine cannot be targeted by lysine methyltransferases.
source: Arginine approximates the charge and steric conformation of lysine, but cannot be targeted by lysine methyltransferases, and therefore represents an appropriate mutation with which to study the PTM-specific functions of H3K36.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of enzyme specificity.

claim: H3K36me3 is catalyzed co-transcriptionally.
source: Because H3K36me3 is catalyzed co-transcriptionally (Kizer et al., 2005), and should therefore track roughly with gene expression, we also took the alternate approach of determining whether gene expression changes in K36R were correlated with the amount of expression normally observed in HWT.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kizer et al., 2005, which provides published evidence for co-transcriptional catalysis of H3K36me3.

claim: SETD2 catalyzes trimethylation of lysine 36 in both the 'canonical' replication-dependent H3 and in the replication-independent histone variant, H3.3.
source: Perhaps more importantly, SETD2 catalyzes trimethylation of lysine 36 in both the 'canonical' replication-dependent H3 and in the replication-independent histone variant, H3.3.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of SETD2 substrate specificity.

claim: H3.3 is thought to play a particularly important role in transcriptionally active regions where H3K36 methylation is enriched.
source: H3.3 is thought to play a particularly important role in transcriptionally active regions where H3K36 methylation is enriched (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002, which provides published evidence for the role of H3.3 in transcriptionally active regions.

claim: A protein with specific affinity for SETD2-catalyzed trimethylation of lysine 36 of the histone H3.3 variant serves as a regulator of RNA pol II elongation.
source: Indeed, a protein with specific affinity for SETD2-catalyzed trimethylation of lysine 36 of the histone H3.3 variant was shown to serve as a regulator of RNA pol II elongation (Wen et al., 2014) and to associate with components of spliceosomal snRNPs to regulate co-transcriptional alternative mRNA splicing (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wen et al., 2014, which provides published evidence for this regulatory role.

claim: A protein with specific affinity for SETD2-catalyzed trimethylation of lysine 36 of the histone H3.3 variant associates with components of spliceosomal snRNPs to regulate co-transcriptional alternative mRNA splicing.
source: Indeed, a protein with specific affinity for SETD2-catalyzed trimethylation of lysine 36 of the histone H3.3 variant was shown to serve as a regulator of RNA pol II elongation (Wen et al., 2014) and to associate with components of spliceosomal snRNPs to regulate co-transcriptional alternative mRNA splicing (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014, which provides published evidence for this regulatory role.

claim: SETD2's prominent association with the C-terminal domain of RNA pol II makes it likely that ablating this protein will result in transcriptional consequences that are unrelated to its catalytic activity.
source: Beyond its other substrates, SETD2's prominent association with the C-terminal domain of RNA pol II (Kizer et al., 2005) makes it likely that ablating this protein will result in transcriptional consequences that are unrelated to its catalytic activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known association of SETD2 with RNA pol II, supported by citation to Kizer et al., 2005, and represents speculation about the consequences of SETD2 ablation.

claim: H3K36me3 depletion in SETD2-mutant renal cell carcinoma has been correlated with defects in transcriptional termination and readthrough into neighboring genes.
source: Interestingly, H3K36me3 depletion in SETD2-mutant renal cell carcinoma has been correlated with defects in transcriptional termination and readthrough into neighboring genes (Grosso et al., 2015), suggesting that H3K36 methylation might influence termination and polyadenylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grosso et al., 2015, which provides published evidence for this correlation.

claim: Dimethylation (N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine, or m6Am) of the nucleotide adjacent to the m7G cap enhances transcript stability.
source: For example, Jaffrey and colleagues recently showed that dimethylation (N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine, or m6Am) of the nucleotide adjacent to the m7G cap enhances transcript stability (Mauer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mauer et al., 2017, which provides published evidence for this mechanism.

claim: The prevailing model for histone PTM modulation of gene expression suggests that it occurs directly proximal to the site of histone modification.
source: The prevailing model for histone PTM modulation of gene expression, reinforced by recent direct evidence (Hilton et al., 2015), suggests that it occurs directly proximal to the site of histone modification.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hilton et al., 2015, which provides published evidence for this model.

claim: Alpha-tubulin was recently identified as a non-histone substrate of SETD2.
source: Notably, alpha-tubulin was recently identified as a non-histone substrate of SETD2 (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Park et al., 2016, which provides published evidence for this substrate identification.

claim: Very low levels of H3K36me3 signal are observed in both western blots from H3K36R mutant larvae and immunofluorescent staining of salivary gland polytene chromosomes.
source: However, this possibility should be tempered by the fact that we observed very low levels of H3K36me3 signal in both western blots from H3K36R mutant larvae (Figure 3A) and immunofluorescent staining of salivary gland polytene chromosomes (McKay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 3A and citation to McKay et al., 2015 for immunofluorescence data.

claim: H3.3 is, at best, a minor contributor to total H3K36me3.
source: Thus H3.3 is, at best, a minor contributor to total H3K36me3.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that very low levels of H3K36me3 remain in H3K36R mutants where only H3.3 could be methylated.

claim: Start-seq signal maps faithfully and robustly, with base-pair resolution, to annotated (observed) transcription start sites (obsTSSs).
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C, Start-seq signal maps faithfully and robustly, with base-pair resolution, to annotated (observed) transcription start sites (obsTSSs), and demarcates sites of high nuclear RNA-seq.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Start-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Start-seq demarcates sites of high nuclear RNA-seq.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C, Start-seq signal maps faithfully and robustly, with base-pair resolution, to annotated (observed) transcription start sites (obsTSSs), and demarcates sites of high nuclear RNA-seq.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of Start-seq and nuclear RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: ATAC-seq signal accumulates most robustly in a window spanning roughly 150 nt upstream, and 50 nt downstream, of obsTSSs.
source: ATAC-seq signal accumulates most robustly in a window spanning roughly 150 nt upstream, and 50 nt downstream, of obsTSSs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Exonic nuTSSs are depleted of ATAC-seq open chromatin signal.
source: Similarly, exonic nuTSSs are depleted of ATAC-seq open chromatin signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The findings do not support a role in Drosophila for H3K36me in suppressing cryptic antisense transcription, as described in yeast.
source: Importantly, these findings do not support a role in Drosophila for H3K36me in suppressing cryptic antisense transcription, as described in yeast.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that antisense transcription does not increase in K36R mutants, in contrast to what has been observed in yeast.

claim: The SETD2 methyltransferase is reported to play a role in regulating alternative splice site choice.
source: The H3K36me3 methyltransferase, SETD2, is reported to play a role in regulating alternative splice site choice (Luco et al., 2010; Pradeepa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luco et al., 2010 and Pradeepa et al., 2012, which provide published evidence for this role.

claim: Studies have implicated H3K36me3 in inefficient intron splicing in clear cell renal cell carcinomas via SETD2 mutation.
source: Furthermore, studies have implicated H3K36me3 in alternative splicing in human cell culture (Luco et al., 2010; Pradeepa et al., 2012) and inefficient intron splicing in clear cell renal cell carcinomas (Simon et al., 2014), again via SETD2 mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Simon et al., 2014, which provides published evidence for this role.

claim: H3K36 is neither a significant contributor to the regulation of alternative splice site choice, nor the efficiency of canonical intron removal.
source: We demonstrate that H3K36 is neither a significant contributor to the regulation of alternative splice site choice, nor the efficiency of canonical intron removal.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MISO and splice junction analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: Methylation of H3K36 does not suppress cryptic transcription in coding regions.
source: We also present evidence that methylation of H3K36 does not suppress cryptic transcription in coding regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Start-seq analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: H4 acetylation is strongly suppressed by H3K36 modification.
source: Interestingly, we confirm that H4 acetylation is strongly suppressed by H3K36 modification, despite the fact that cryptic transcripts do not appear.
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cryptic transcripts do not appear in H3K36R mutants despite increased H4 acetylation.
source: Interestingly, we confirm that H4 acetylation is strongly suppressed by H3K36 modification, despite the fact that cryptic transcripts do not appear.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Start-seq analysis shown in Figure 4 combined with the western blot data in Figure 3A.

claim: The finding argues for an uncoupling of H4ac levels from cryptic initiation in coding regions in metazoans.
source: This finding argues for an uncoupling of H4ac levels from cryptic initiation in coding regions in metazoans, and suggests that the suppression of cryptic transcription initiation in multicellular organisms may be more complex than previously appreciated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that H4 acetylation increases in K36R mutants without a corresponding increase in cryptic transcription.

claim: The suppression of cryptic transcription initiation in multicellular organisms may be more complex than previously appreciated.
source: This finding argues for an uncoupling of H4ac levels from cryptic initiation in coding regions in metazoans, and suggests that the suppression of cryptic transcription initiation in multicellular organisms may be more complex than previously appreciated.
evidence: This claim represents speculation based on the unexpected finding that H4 hyperacetylation does not lead to cryptic transcription in Drosophila.

claim: H3K36 is required for proper mRNA maturation, providing a post-transcriptional benefit across a range of highly expressed genes.
source: Finally, we present evidence that H3K36 is required for proper mRNA maturation, providing a post-transcriptional benefit across a range of highly expressed genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of poly-A and nuclear RNA-seq data and the rescue experiments with RNA degradation factors shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mRNA 'fitness' benefit provided by H3K36 is linked to the efficiency of 3' end formation or polyadenylation.
source: Our genetic suppression data suggest that this mRNA 'fitness' benefit is somehow linked to the efficiency of 3' end formation or polyadenylation (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue of gene expression by deadenylase depletion and the observation of reduced poly-A tail length in K36R mutants, as shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The enrichment of H3K36me3 at the 3' ends of genes makes it a likely candidate to interface with termination and polyadenylation activities.
source: Indeed, the enrichment of H3K36me3 at the 3' ends of genes makes it a likely candidate to interface with these activities.
evidence: This claim represents speculation based on the known distribution of H3K36me3 and the observed polyadenylation defects.

claim: H3K36 modification might recruit some type of RNA modifying enzyme.
source: Another possibility is that H3K36 modification might recruit some type of RNA modifying enzyme.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about potential mechanisms by which H3K36 might affect mRNA stability.

claim: H3K36 might contribute to mRNA maturation across multiple processing steps, with the combined effect of protecting target mRNAs from surveillance and eventual degradation.
source: Moreover, H3K36 might contribute to mRNA maturation across multiple processing steps, with the combined effect of protecting target mRNAs from surveillance and eventual degradation.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about the potential mechanism by which H3K36 affects mRNA stability.

claim: The rate of transcribing polymerase through nucleosomes that are modified at H3K36 might change in K36R mutants.
source: For example, it is possible that the rate of transcribing polymerase through nucleosomes that are modified at H3K36 might change, and therefore the capping, cleavage and polyadenylation machinery that associates with the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II (Ho et al., 1998; McCracken et al., 1997) might become improperly distributed in K36R mutants.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about potential indirect mechanisms by which H3K36 might affect gene expression, supported by citations about RNA processing machinery.

claim: The capping, cleavage and polyadenylation machinery associates with the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II.
source: For example, it is possible that the rate of transcribing polymerase through nucleosomes that are modified at H3K36 might change, and therefore the capping, cleavage and polyadenylation machinery that associates with the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II (Ho et al., 1998; McCracken et al., 1997) might become improperly distributed in K36R mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ho et al., 1998 and McCracken et al., 1997, which provide published evidence for this association.

claim: H3K36me's previously reported role in three-dimensional genome organization might extend to the concentration of factors related to mRNA maturation at sites of active transcription.
source: Finally, H3K36me's previously reported role in three-dimensional genome organization (Evans et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; Ulianov et al., 2016) might extend to the concentration of factors related to mRNA maturation at sites of active transcription, which would be impaired upon H3K36 mutation.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about potential mechanisms by which H3K36 might affect gene expression, supported by citations about 3D genome organization.
